query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of AlCoCrFeNi HEA is the fabrication of protective coatings [,]. HEA-based coatings, deposited on medium-carbon steel substrates, can considerably enhance the material performances, extend service life, and reduce product costs [,,]. Thick coatings with low porosity and a high level of adhesion can be produced via the high velocity fuel spraying (HVOF) technique [,]. HVOF is a combustion spray process in which a hydrocarbon fuel (kerosene, methane, propane, etc.) is ignited, mixing with oxygen to accelerate feedstock powder towards the substrate [,]. Depending on the particle’s size and location in the high-temperature flow, the particles undergo various transformations, such as melting, softening, spheroidization, precipitation, and surface or total oxidation, similar to those observed with the atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) method []. Lower particle temperatures than those achieved in plasma spraying and higher particle speeds result in lower in-flight particle oxidation and better coating densities.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 shows the difference in the properties based on the spraying distance. As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. With an increase in the spraying distance, the particles are exposed to oxygen for a longer time, which leads to an increased content of oxides (Figure 4d). As the particles oxidize with the formation of alumina, BCC solid solution loses aluminum, which is reflected in a decrease in its lattice parameter (Figure 3b). Prior to spraying, the feedstock powder was dried in an oven at 200 °C for 3 h to remove the moisture and improve its flowability. First, 316 stainless steel cylindrical specimens with dimensions of Φ 25 × 7 mm were used as substrates. Before spraying, the substrates were cleaned with an ultrasonic cleaner in acetone for 10 min, and then dried with a dryer. To improve the bonding strength of the coating, sand blasting one side of the substrate was carried out to obtain a certain cleanliness and roughness. During sand blasting, an Al2O3 particle with a size of less than 1.25 mm was used as an abrasive. The substrates were sandblasted under a compressed air pressure of about 0.5 MPa for 30 s. An APS system (3710, PRAXAIR SURFACE TECHNOLOGIES, Indianapolis, IN, USA) with a high-energy plasma gun (SG-100) was employed to deposit the coating. decision.rationale: Both directions A and C address the problem of inadequate coating thickness and have physically sound mechanisms. Direction A focuses on optimizing the spray distance, while direction C focuses on increasing the particle velocity. By merging these two directions, we can optimize both the spray distance and particle velocity to achieve thicker, more adherent coatings with minimal as-sprayed oxidation. The merged direction respects the material system and operating conditions, and the evidence from earlier MCrAlY bond coat studies using the M3 system supports the intervention.
